opus-5.5.text:
I think it's pretty underinvested in, honestly. If you look at how much effort goes into questions like "how fast does AI progress go once AIs can substantially automate AI research," it's a tiny number of people — maybe a few dozen doing serious work on it, and many of them only part-time. And yet that question is one of the most decision-relevant ones out there. Whether we get something like a software-only intelligence explosion that goes from roughly human-level AI researchers to vastly superhuman systems in months, versus a slower transition over many years, changes a lot about what interventions make sense, how much warning we get, how much time we'll have to use AI to help with safety work, and how governments should be thinking about this.

Part of why it's neglected is that it's genuinely hard and kind of awkward as a field. You're trying to reason about returns to AI R&D, how compute and algorithmic progress trade off, whether there are diminishing returns to ideas, how parallelizable research is — and the empirical evidence is thin and noisy. People do things like look at historical algorithmic efficiency gains and try to estimate how much progress you get per doubling of research effort, but those estimates have big error bars. So it doesn't fit neatly into academic incentives, and it doesn't fit neatly into what labs are paid to do either.

That said, I'd distinguish between quantity and quality. I think the marginal careful person working on this could add a lot, especially if they're grounded in actual ML research practice — understanding what bottlenecks AI researchers really hit, how much of progress comes from compute-heavy experiments versus insight, that kind of thing. Some of the existing work is more armchair than I'd like. So my overall take is: more people, more empirical grounding, and more effort to connect the forecasts to concrete decisions — like what level of AI R&D automation should trigger which safety measures. That seems quite valuable relative to where we are now.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a months-long jump from roughly human-level AI researchers to vastly superhuman systems with a transition over many years, and says that difference changes important decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's just wildly under-resourced relative to how much it matters. If you buy the basic picture — that at some point AI systems will be able to do AI research themselves, and that this could compress what would otherwise be decades of progress into a few years or less — then the question of how fast that goes, and what the dynamics look like, is maybe the single most decision-relevant question for anyone working on this. And yet the number of people who are seriously working on it full time is… I don't know, a handful? You've got the Epoch folks, you've got Tom Davidson's work on takeoff speeds, Daniel Kokotajlo and the AI Futures crowd, a few others. You could probably fit everyone doing careful quantitative work on this in one room, and it wouldn't be a very big room.

And I want to be clear that I'm not saying the work that exists is bad. Tom's compute-centric model was genuinely useful to me — it gave me a framework for actually thinking about the question rather than just gesturing at "intelligence explosion" as a vibe. But the amount of effort is tiny compared to, say, the amount of effort that goes into capabilities research, or even compared to the amount that goes into various kinds of alignment research. And a lot of alignment work implicitly depends on takeoff assumptions. If you think we'll have five years between "AI can automate most AI R&D" and "AI is vastly superhuman," you should be doing very different things than if you think it's five months.

I'd also say the research that exists is skewed toward a particular style — macro models, extrapolating compute trends, that kind of thing. There's much less work on the more mechanistic questions: what actually happens inside a lab when you have a million AI researchers running at fifty times human speed? What are the actual bottlenecks — compute for experiments, serial time, taste, coordination? I've tried to think about some of this myself, and my honest impression is that the uncertainty is enormous and that we're not doing nearly enough to shrink it. I think it's plausible you could get a lot of value from a few more careful people spending a couple years on this, and that's a pretty unusual situation for an important question.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s surprisingly little, given how consequential the question is. There’s a lot of discussion of takeoff speeds, but much less work that tries to build a quantitative model, make the assumptions explicit, and see which assumptions actually drive the answer.

In particular, I’d like to see more work on the feedback loop from AI automating AI research: how much does that accelerate progress, what bottlenecks remain, and how does that change as the systems get more capable? You don’t need to think we can forecast this precisely to think that understanding those mechanisms would be useful.

So my overall view is that this is underinvested in. There’s substantial uncertainty, but that’s partly a reason to do the research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s surprisingly little, given how consequential the question is. Whether AI progress accelerates over a few months or over a decade makes a big difference to what safety work is useful and what kinds of policy responses are feasible.

I’d particularly like to see more work that breaks the question into concrete pieces. How much can AI accelerate AI research? Where do experiments, compute, and other bottlenecks start to matter? How quickly can improvements actually be deployed? You can make progress on those questions without having a complete model of the whole process.

I wouldn’t expect that work to give us a very precise takeoff date or speed. But even identifying which assumptions drive the answer, and what evidence would change our minds, seems pretty valuable.
